cases.stem: Altostrat's editorial and rights systems in the leased data centre reach Google Cloud over a single 1 Gbps IPsec VPN tunnel, and editorial outages have stalled publishing. They need resilient private connectivity with a supported availability SLA and predictable throughput. What should you propose?

options.t: Two Dedicated Interconnect connections in the same metropolitan area, in two different edge availability domains, with VLAN attachments and Cloud Router using BGP
A second Classic VPN tunnel to the same Cloud VPN gateway
Increasing the existing tunnel's bandwidth to 10 Gbps
Direct Peering with Google at an internet exchange

cases.explanation: Two Dedicated Interconnect connections placed in two edge availability domains within a metro is the supported 99.9% topology, and it delivers private, predictable-throughput connectivity that does not traverse the public internet. Cloud Router exchanges routes dynamically over BGP so failover is automatic.

why_wrong.B: Classic VPN is legacy and offers a lower SLA; more importantly, additional tunnels still traverse the public internet with variable throughput.
why_wrong.C: An IPsec tunnel's throughput is capped per tunnel regardless of the underlying link, and a single tunnel remains a single point of failure - which is the actual problem.
why_wrong.D: Direct Peering gives access to Google public IPs but does not connect to a VPC, carries no SLA, and cannot reach internal resources.

cases.stem: Altostrat runs Cloud Monitoring for its GKE estate and self-hosted Prometheus and Grafana for the data-centre applications, and wants a single pane of glass without rewriting existing Prometheus instrumentation or losing its Grafana dashboards. What should you recommend?

options.t: Adopt Google Cloud Managed Service for Prometheus, keeping PromQL and existing exporters, and point Grafana at it as a data source alongside Cloud Monitoring metrics
Replace all Prometheus exporters with the Ops Agent and rebuild every dashboard in Cloud Monitoring
Scale up the self-hosted Prometheus cluster and forward Cloud Monitoring metrics into it
Send all metrics to BigQuery and build dashboards in Looker Studio

cases.explanation: Managed Service for Prometheus is a drop-in managed backend that keeps PromQL, existing exporters, and Grafana dashboards while removing the burden of running Prometheus at scale, and it stores data in Monarch alongside Cloud Monitoring metrics so both can be queried together.

why_wrong.B: This discards working instrumentation and dashboards for no functional gain and is a large migration project.
why_wrong.C: This keeps Altostrat operating Prometheus themselves, which is the toil they are trying to remove, and adds a fragile export path.
why_wrong.D: BigQuery is not a time-series monitoring backend; alerting latency and query cost make it unsuitable for operational metrics.

cases.stem: Altostrat must filter inappropriate or non-compliant material before publication, and must guard the subscriber-facing conversational agent against prompt injection and data leakage. Which two controls should the design include? (Choose 2.)

options.t: Model Armor screening prompts and responses on the conversational agent for prompt injection, jailbreak attempts, and unsafe content
Sensitive Data Protection inspection of generated summaries and extracted metadata before publication, to detect and redact personal data
Cloud Armor rate limiting on the agent endpoint
Binary Authorization on the GKE clusters hosting the agent

cases.explanation: Model Armor is the control designed for LLM-layer threats, inspecting both directions of the conversation. Sensitive Data Protection handles the content-compliance half - archive material and generated summaries will contain names and other personal data that must be detected and redacted before publication.

why_wrong.C: Rate limiting is worth having for abuse and cost control, but it does not inspect prompt or response content, which is what the requirement asks for.
why_wrong.D: Binary Authorization governs which container images may run. It is good supply-chain hygiene but does not address content moderation or prompt injection.

cases.stem: A rights holder disputes an AI-generated licensing price and demands to know how the decision was reached. Altostrat must be able to explain and audit any AI-driven decision affecting rights, pricing, or moderation. Which combination best satisfies this?

options.t: Register every model version in Vertex AI Model Registry, enable Vertex Explainable AI feature attributions on the pricing model, log every prediction request and response with its model version, and retain Cloud Audit Logs for the serving project
Store the model's training dataset in Cloud Storage with versioning enabled
Publish the model's source code to an internal repository
Add a disclaimer to the licensing portal stating that prices are generated automatically

cases.explanation: Auditability requires reconstructing a specific past decision: which model version produced it, on what input, and which features drove the output. Model Registry gives version lineage, Explainable AI gives per-prediction feature attributions, request-response logging captures the actual inputs and outputs, and audit logs record who accessed and changed what.

why_wrong.B: Dataset versioning is a useful component of reproducibility but does not explain an individual prediction.
why_wrong.C: Source code shows the algorithm, not why this input produced that price with the model weights in effect at the time.
why_wrong.D: A disclaimer is a legal notice, not an explanation, and does not satisfy an audit requirement.

cases.stem: Altostrat needs to extract structured metadata - speakers, topics, locations, and on-screen entities - from a 40-year archive of audio and video, and to generate episode summaries and chapter markers. Which pipeline design is most appropriate?

options.t: Trigger a pipeline on object finalisation in Cloud Storage that runs Speech-to-Text for transcription and Video Intelligence API for shot, label, and on-screen text detection, then passes the transcript and detections to a Gemini model for summarisation and chaptering, writing results to BigQuery
Train a custom multimodal model from scratch on the archive before processing any content
Have editorial staff watch and tag the archive, using AI only for new content
Run a single Gemini prompt over each raw multi-hour media file with no preprocessing and no schema

cases.explanation: This composes purpose-built prebuilt APIs with a generative model for the language task: Speech-to-Text produces timestamped transcripts, Video Intelligence supplies shot boundaries, labels, and OCR of on-screen text, and Gemini turns those structured inputs into summaries and chapter markers. Event-driven triggering handles both backfill and new ingest.

why_wrong.B: Training a multimodal model from scratch is enormously expensive and unnecessary when prebuilt APIs cover the perception tasks - exam guide 2.5 favours prebuilt solutions where they fit.
why_wrong.C: Manual tagging of a 40-year archive is the cost problem Altostrat is trying to solve.
why_wrong.D: Passing raw multi-hour media with no preprocessing or output schema gives inconsistent, unstructured results and no timestamps for chaptering.

cases.stem: Subscribers and licensing customers must be able to find archive material conversationally, with answers grounded in Altostrat's own catalogue and citations back to the source recording. What should you build on?

options.t: Vertex AI Search, indexing the catalogue and extracted metadata as a data store, with grounded responses and citations
A Gemini model prompted with the user's question and no access to the catalogue
A BigQuery full-text search over the metadata table exposed through a web form
Fine-tuning a foundation model on the entire catalogue so the knowledge is in the weights

cases.explanation: Vertex AI Search provides retrieval-augmented generation over your own data: it indexes the corpus, retrieves relevant passages for each query, and grounds the generated answer in them with citations. Grounding with citations is exactly what a licensing customer needs to trust and verify the result.

why_wrong.B: An ungrounded model has no knowledge of Altostrat's private catalogue and will hallucinate titles and details.
why_wrong.C: Full-text search returns rows, not conversational answers, and cannot handle natural-language intent or follow-up questions.
why_wrong.D: Fine-tuning teaches style and format far better than it teaches facts, produces no citations, and requires retraining every time the catalogue changes.

cases.stem: Altostrat's GKE estate spans two regions and is growing, and the platform team cannot keep applying policy and configuration cluster by cluster. They want consistent policy, config, and version management across all clusters from one place. What should you recommend?

options.t: Register the clusters into a GKE fleet and use Config Sync and Policy Controller to apply configuration and policy from a Git repository, with fleet-level upgrade management
Write a shell script that loops over clusters running kubectl apply
Consolidate all workloads into a single very large cluster
Give each application team full admin on its own cluster and publish a standards document

cases.explanation: Fleet management with Config Sync gives GitOps-based configuration delivery to many clusters, and Policy Controller enforces guardrails as admission policy. This is the managed answer to per-cluster toil and matches the scaling requirement without collapsing failure domains.

why_wrong.B: A kubectl loop has no drift detection, no reconciliation, and no policy enforcement; clusters diverge silently.
why_wrong.C: A single cluster removes the regional isolation that protects Altostrat's reliability requirement and creates a very large blast radius.
why_wrong.D: A standards document is not an enforcement mechanism, and full cluster admin per team guarantees divergence.

cases.stem: Altostrat staff authenticate through Google Workspace, while partners and licensees use a third-party OIDC provider. Partners need access to specific Google Cloud resources without Altostrat creating and managing Google identities for them. What should you implement?

options.t: Workforce Identity Federation, federating the third-party OIDC provider so partner users receive short-lived credentials mapped to IAM roles
Create a Cloud Identity user account for every partner user and synchronise passwords
Share a single service account key with each partner organisation
Grant allUsers the required IAM roles and restrict access with Cloud Armor by source IP

cases.explanation: Workforce Identity Federation is designed for human users from an external identity provider. Partner users sign in with their own IdP, and Google Cloud issues short-lived credentials with IAM roles mapped from their identity or group claims, so Altostrat never provisions or manages Google accounts for them.

why_wrong.B: Provisioning Google identities for every partner user is exactly the management burden the requirement excludes, and synchronising passwords is poor practice.
why_wrong.C: A shared long-lived key destroys per-user attribution and can be copied freely.
why_wrong.D: Granting allUsers makes the resource public; IP restrictions are not an identity control and fail for remote partner staff.

cases.stem: Cymbal's supplier feeds arrive by SFTP and are processed by a nightly Perl ETL job; a failed run leaves the catalogue stale for 24 hours. They must move to continuous ingestion. Which design should you propose?

options.t: Land supplier files in Cloud Storage, emit an object-finalise notification to Pub/Sub, and process each file with a streaming Dataflow pipeline that writes to the catalogue store, with a dead-letter topic for failures
Keep the nightly job but run it on a larger Compute Engine VM
Run the Perl job every 15 minutes with Cloud Scheduler
Have suppliers write directly into the production MongoDB catalogue over the internet

cases.explanation: Object-triggered notifications turn each supplier delivery into an event, so a file is processed on arrival rather than waiting for a nightly window. Dataflow handles per-file scale and retries, and a dead-letter topic means one malformed supplier feed no longer blocks the whole catalogue - which is the actual failure mode described.

why_wrong.B: A bigger VM makes the nightly job faster but keeps the 24-hour staleness window and the single-point-of-failure batch design.
why_wrong.C: More frequent batch runs reduce staleness but retain the all-or-nothing failure behaviour and add scheduling contention.
why_wrong.D: Direct supplier writes to a production database over the internet is a severe security and data-integrity risk with no validation stage.

cases.stem: Cymbal must derive structured product attributes - material, dimensions, colour, compatibility - from inconsistent free-text supplier descriptions across 4 million SKUs, and needs the output to conform to a fixed attribute schema for the catalogue. What is the most appropriate approach?

options.t: Use a Gemini model with a constrained response schema (structured output) and few-shot examples, batching descriptions through Vertex AI, and route low-confidence extractions to human review
Write regular expressions for each of the 2,800 suppliers' formats
Ask suppliers to resubmit all data in Cymbal's schema before onboarding
Train a separate custom classification model per attribute from scratch

cases.explanation: Attribute extraction from heterogeneous free text is a natural language task that generative models handle well, and constraining the response to a schema is what makes the output usable in a catalogue rather than free prose. Routing low-confidence results to the existing review team implements the required human-in-the-loop step.

why_wrong.B: Maintaining regex sets for 2,800 suppliers whose formats change is unmanageable, and it is what the 90-person team effectively does today.
why_wrong.C: Requiring resubmission pushes the problem to suppliers and conflicts with the goal of onboarding a supplier in hours.
why_wrong.D: Building and maintaining a bespoke model per attribute is far more expensive and slower than prompting a foundation model with a schema.

cases.stem: Cymbal wants to generate additional product image variants - alternate backgrounds and colourways - instead of commissioning new photography. Which Google Cloud capability directly supports this?

options.t: Imagen on Vertex AI, using image editing capabilities such as background replacement and masked inpainting on the supplier's original photograph
The Cloud Vision API's image properties endpoint
Cloud Storage image transformation with gsutil
Video Intelligence API label detection

cases.explanation: Imagen provides generation and editing, including background replacement and mask-based inpainting, which is exactly the described requirement of producing background and colour variants from an existing product photograph while preserving the product itself.

why_wrong.B: Vision's image properties returns analysis such as dominant colours and crop hints; it does not generate or edit images.
why_wrong.C: gsutil is a storage transfer tool and performs no image processing at all.
why_wrong.D: Video Intelligence analyses video content and is unrelated to still-image generation.

cases.stem: Cymbal's new conversational shopping agent will place orders, and cardholder data is in scope for PCI DSS. Which architectural decision most effectively limits PCI DSS audit scope?

options.t: Tokenise card data at capture through a PCI-compliant payment provider so the agent and application never store, process, or transmit the primary account number, and isolate any remaining cardholder data environment in its own project behind a VPC Service Controls perimeter
Encrypt the card number with CMEK before storing it in the orders database
Restrict access to the orders database to a small group of administrators
Log all card numbers to Cloud Logging with a customer-managed retention policy for auditability

cases.explanation: PCI DSS scope follows the primary account number. If tokenisation means your systems never store, process, or transmit it, those systems fall out of scope, which is by far the biggest reduction in audit burden. Whatever cardholder data environment remains is isolated in its own project with a service perimeter to contain scope.

why_wrong.B: Encrypting the PAN keeps it in your environment, so the system remains in scope; encryption is a control within scope, not a way out of it.
why_wrong.C: Access restriction is a required control but does nothing to reduce which systems are in scope.
why_wrong.D: Writing card numbers into logs dramatically expands scope and is a direct PCI DSS violation.

cases.stem: Cymbal's storefront must absorb seasonal peaks running eight times baseline traffic without over-provisioning for the rest of the year. The current PHP and Java applications run on fixed-size VM pools. Which target design best meets this?

options.t: Containerise the storefront and run it on Cloud Run or GKE with horizontal autoscaling, front it with a global external Application Load Balancer and Cloud CDN, and move session state to Memorystore
Provision VM pools sized for peak traffic year-round to guarantee capacity
Keep the fixed pools and add a manual runbook to add VMs when traffic rises
Move the storefront to a single very large machine type with vertical autoscaling

cases.explanation: Horizontal autoscaling on a serverless or managed container platform matches capacity to demand, CDN offloads static and cacheable content so origin scaling is smaller, and externalising session state to Memorystore is the prerequisite that makes instances disposable and horizontal scaling possible.

why_wrong.B: Sizing for peak year-round is the cost problem the requirement explicitly rules out.
why_wrong.C: Manual scaling cannot react fast enough to an 8x seasonal spike and depends on someone being awake.
why_wrong.D: Vertical scaling has a hard ceiling at the largest machine type and leaves a single point of failure.

cases.stem: Cymbal's product catalogue currently lives in self-managed MongoDB and its cart and session data in self-managed Redis. They want managed equivalents with minimal application rewriting. Which pair should you recommend?

options.t: Firestore in Datastore or Native mode for the catalogue documents, and Memorystore for Redis for cart and session data
Bigtable for the catalogue and Cloud SQL for sessions
BigQuery for the catalogue and Firestore for sessions
Spanner for both the catalogue and the sessions

cases.explanation: Memorystore for Redis is protocol-compatible with Redis, so cart and session code generally needs only a connection-string change. Firestore is Google Cloud's managed document database and is the closest managed analogue to MongoDB for catalogue documents. Note that MongoDB Atlas on Google Cloud is also a valid answer when full MongoDB API compatibility is required.

why_wrong.B: Bigtable is a wide-column store with no document queries or secondary indexes, and Cloud SQL is a poor fit for high-churn session data.
why_wrong.C: BigQuery is an analytical warehouse, unsuited to per-request catalogue lookups.
why_wrong.D: Spanner is excellent for transactional relational data but is a costly and awkward fit for ephemeral session caching, and it is not a document store.

cases.stem: Cymbal requires that AI-enriched catalogue data is reviewed by a person before publication, but reviewing all 4 million SKUs manually would defeat the purpose. What review design should you recommend?

options.t: Publish automatically above a calibrated confidence threshold, queue only low-confidence or high-value items for human review, and sample a random percentage of auto-published items to monitor quality over time
Queue every enriched item for human review before publication
Publish everything automatically and correct items only when a customer complains
Have reviewers check the first 1,000 items, then disable review permanently

cases.explanation: Confidence-based routing concentrates scarce human attention where the model is uncertain or the commercial stakes are high, while random sampling of auto-published items gives an ongoing measurement of true quality. Without that sampling you have no way to detect model drift.

why_wrong.B: Reviewing everything reproduces the manual bottleneck the programme exists to remove.
why_wrong.C: Customer complaints are a slow, damaging, and biased quality signal.
why_wrong.D: A one-off check gives no ongoing quality signal, and model or supplier-data drift will go undetected.

cases.stem: Cymbal wants on-site product discovery that understands natural-language queries such as 'a waterproof jacket for hiking that works with my existing rain trousers', with relevance tuned for retail and support for browse, recommendations, and personalisation. Which product is the intended fit?

options.t: Vertex AI Search for commerce (Discovery AI for retail)
A BigQuery LIKE query across product titles
Cloud Search over the corporate intranet
The Natural Language API entity extraction endpoint

cases.explanation: Vertex AI Search for commerce is Google's retail-specific search and discovery product, built on the same technology as Google Search and tuned for catalogue relevance, browse, recommendations, and personalisation from user events.

why_wrong.B: Keyword matching cannot interpret intent, attributes, or compatibility relationships expressed in natural language.
why_wrong.C: Cloud Search indexes enterprise content for employees, not customer-facing product catalogues.
why_wrong.D: The Natural Language API extracts entities and sentiment from text; it is not a search or ranking system.

cases.stem: EHR Healthcare must maintain 99.9% availability for its customer-facing applications after migrating off the colocation facilities. The applications are already containerised. Which target architecture best supports this objective?

options.t: Regional GKE clusters with node pools across at least three zones, workloads deployed with multiple replicas and pod anti-affinity, behind a global external Application Load Balancer
A single zonal GKE cluster with a large node pool and cluster autoscaling
Compute Engine VMs in one zone with a managed instance group and health checks
Cloud Run in a single region with minimum instances set to zero

cases.explanation: A regional GKE cluster replicates the control plane and spreads nodes across zones, so a zone failure does not take out the cluster. Multiple replicas with anti-affinity ensures pods are not co-located on one node or zone, and the global load balancer provides a single entry point with health-checked failover.

why_wrong.B: A zonal cluster has a single-zone control plane; a zone outage takes down the whole cluster, which cannot support 99.9%.
why_wrong.C: A single-zone MIG fails for the same reason, and it also abandons the existing container investment.
why_wrong.D: A single region with min instances zero adds cold-start latency and provides no regional redundancy; it also does not fit the existing Kubernetes estate.

cases.stem: Several of EHR Healthcare's insurance providers refuse to change their integration method, which uses scheduled SFTP file drops. EHR must keep onboarding new providers quickly while supporting these legacy partners. What should you design?

options.t: Keep an SFTP-compatible ingestion endpoint that lands files in Cloud Storage, and build a standard event-driven ingestion pipeline behind it that all providers - legacy and new - feed into, exposing a documented API for new providers
Require all providers, including legacy ones, to adopt a new REST API before migration completes
Maintain a permanent parallel legacy stack in the colocation facility for the SFTP providers
Write a bespoke integration for each provider as they are onboarded

cases.explanation: The pattern is to preserve the legacy interface at the edge while standardising everything behind it. Files land in Cloud Storage, an object-finalise event drives the same normalisation pipeline used by API-based providers, and new providers get a documented API. This satisfies both the legacy constraint and the fast-onboarding requirement with one pipeline.

why_wrong.B: The case states these providers will not change; a migration plan that depends on them changing will fail.
why_wrong.C: A permanent parallel stack in the colocation facility conflicts with the lease expiry and the cost-reduction objective.
why_wrong.D: Bespoke per-provider integrations are precisely what makes onboarding slow today.

cases.stem: EHR Healthcare manages users in Microsoft Active Directory and wants staff to use their existing corporate credentials for Google Cloud, with group membership driving IAM. What should you implement?

options.t: Provision identities into Cloud Identity using Google Cloud Directory Sync or Directory Provisioning, configure SAML SSO against the existing identity provider, and bind IAM roles to the synchronised groups
Create Google accounts manually for each employee and ask them to choose new passwords
Replicate the Active Directory domain controllers into Google Cloud and join all resources to the domain
Use Workload Identity Federation for employee sign-in

cases.explanation: Directory synchronisation creates and maintains the Cloud Identity accounts and groups from Active Directory as the source of truth, SAML SSO means authentication still happens against the corporate identity provider, and binding IAM to synchronised groups keeps joiner/mover/leaver handling in AD.

why_wrong.B: Manual account creation with separate passwords creates a second identity store that immediately drifts and weakens offboarding.
why_wrong.C: Running domain controllers in Google Cloud may be needed for some Windows workloads, but it does not by itself give Google Cloud console and IAM access using corporate credentials.
why_wrong.D: Workload Identity Federation is for workloads and non-human identities. For employees, Workforce Identity Federation or SAML SSO with Cloud Identity is the correct mechanism.

cases.stem: EHR Healthcare must maintain regulatory compliance for protected health information throughout the migration and afterwards. Which two measures are most directly relevant? (Choose 2.)

options.t: Execute a Business Associate Agreement with Google Cloud and restrict the architecture to services covered by it
Enable Data Access audit logs for services handling PHI and route them to a log bucket with a retention period matching the regulatory requirement
Enable Cloud CDN in front of the clinical application to improve performance
Store PHI in a single project with roles/editor granted to the whole engineering team for operational agility

cases.explanation: A BAA is the contractual foundation for handling PHI on Google Cloud, and it covers a defined list of services, so the architecture must stay within it. Data Access audit logs record who read PHI - these are off by default for most services and must be explicitly enabled - and they must be retained for the regulatory period to be useful in an audit.

why_wrong.C: Caching a clinical application at edge nodes risks caching PHI in shared infrastructure, which makes the compliance position worse rather than better.
why_wrong.D: Broad editor access to PHI violates least privilege and minimum-necessary access principles central to health data regulation.

cases.stem: EHR Healthcare's incidents are typically reported by customers before the operations team notices, because each colocation site has its own monitoring tools with no aggregated view. What should you implement as the target state?

options.t: Centralise metrics, logs, and traces in Google Cloud Observability across all environments, define SLOs for the customer-facing applications, and alert on error-budget burn rate
Standardise all sites on the same self-hosted open-source monitoring stack
Add a customer-facing status page so customers can report issues faster
Increase the frequency of manual health checks to hourly

cases.explanation: The business requirement is centralised visibility of the performance of all deployed applications. Consolidating telemetry into one platform and defining SLOs on user-facing indicators means the team is alerted by symptoms of customer impact rather than learning about them from customers.

why_wrong.B: Standardising the self-hosted stack improves consistency but keeps EHR operating monitoring infrastructure and does not by itself produce SLO-based alerting.
why_wrong.C: A status page communicates during incidents; it does not detect them.
why_wrong.D: Hourly manual checks still leave up to an hour of undetected impact and do not scale.

cases.stem: EHR Healthcare wants to derive insights on industry and healthcare trends from data across all its customers. Which design satisfies this while respecting patient privacy?

options.t: Land operational data in BigQuery, use Sensitive Data Protection to de-identify direct and quasi-identifiers into an analytics dataset, and grant analysts access only to the de-identified dataset through authorised views
Grant analysts direct read access to the production clinical databases
Export raw patient records to a Cloud Storage bucket shared with an external analytics vendor
Aggregate the data manually into spreadsheets each quarter

cases.explanation: This separates the operational and analytical estates, applies de-identification before analysts see the data, and uses authorised views so analysts query derived results without access to the underlying identified tables. That combination meets the analytics requirement without expanding PHI access.

why_wrong.B: Direct analyst access to production clinical data violates minimum-necessary access and puts analytical query load on operational systems.
why_wrong.C: Exporting raw records to a third party without de-identification is a serious compliance breach.
why_wrong.D: Manual quarterly spreadsheets do not scale, are error-prone, and still involve handling identified data.

cases.stem: EHR Healthcare runs Microsoft SQL Server for billing and claims, with stored procedures and SQL Server Agent jobs the team wants to keep. The lease on the hosting facility expires in 14 months. What is the most appropriate migration target?

options.t: Cloud SQL for SQL Server, using Database Migration Service for a minimal-downtime migration
Rewrite the billing schema and procedures for Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL
BigQuery, since billing and claims data is analytical
Firestore, to remove the relational dependency

cases.explanation: Cloud SQL for SQL Server keeps the engine, so stored procedures and Agent jobs carry across with minimal change, and Database Migration Service provides continuous replication for a low-downtime cutover. With a 14-month lease clock, a like-for-like managed migration is the pragmatic disposition.

why_wrong.B: A schema and procedure rewrite is a long, risky project that does not fit the timeline and delivers no benefit the business has asked for.
why_wrong.C: Billing and claims is a transactional OLTP workload; BigQuery is not a transactional database.
why_wrong.D: Firestore has no relational joins or transactions of the shape this workload needs and would require a full application rewrite.

cases.stem: During the migration period, EHR Healthcare needs a secure, reliable, high-performance connection between the remaining colocation facilities and Google Cloud, carrying replication traffic for several databases. Bandwidth requirements are in the multi-gigabit range and consistent. What should you recommend?

options.t: Dedicated Interconnect with redundant connections and Cloud Router, sized for the replication traffic
HA VPN over the internet, which is sufficient for any replication workload
Partner Interconnect with a single 50 Mbps VLAN attachment
Storage Transfer Service over the public internet

cases.explanation: Sustained multi-gigabit, latency-sensitive replication traffic containing PHI calls for private connectivity with predictable throughput. Dedicated Interconnect provides that at 10 or 100 Gbps per connection, and redundant connections with Cloud Router give automatic failover during the migration window.

why_wrong.B: HA VPN tunnels have per-tunnel throughput limits (around 3 Gbps aggregate depending on configuration) and traverse the public internet with variable latency - not appropriate as a blanket answer for multi-gigabit database replication.
why_wrong.C: 50 Mbps is orders of magnitude short of the stated requirement, and a single attachment has no redundancy.
why_wrong.D: Storage Transfer Service moves objects between storage systems; it is not a network connectivity solution for database replication.

cases.stem: KnightMotives ingests telemetry from 900,000 vehicles through self-managed MQTT brokers on VMs, which have failed repeatedly under regional traffic spikes. They need reliable, elastic ingestion that absorbs spikes without loss. What should you recommend?

options.t: Publish telemetry to Pub/Sub, which buffers and scales automatically, and consume with Dataflow for processing and fan-out to storage
Add more MQTT broker VMs behind a passthrough Network Load Balancer with a fixed instance count
Have vehicles write directly to Bigtable using service account keys embedded in the telematics units
Batch telemetry on the vehicle and upload once daily to Cloud Storage

cases.explanation: Pub/Sub is a globally scalable, durable message buffer that absorbs traffic spikes without capacity planning, decoupling producers from consumers so a slow downstream system causes backlog rather than data loss. Dataflow then processes and fans out to the serving and analytics stores.

why_wrong.B: A fixed instance count is exactly what fails under spikes, and KnightMotives still operates the broker fleet.
why_wrong.C: Embedding long-lived credentials in 900,000 field devices is an unmanageable security exposure, and direct writes provide no buffering.
why_wrong.D: Daily batch upload makes sub-second safety alerting impossible, contradicting a core business requirement.

cases.stem: KnightMotives requires safety-critical alerts to reach the driver within one second of the triggering event, and vehicles routinely operate with intermittent or no connectivity. What does this imply for the architecture?

options.t: Safety inference must run on the vehicle or at the depot edge, with the cloud used for training, model distribution, and aggregate analytics rather than in the alerting path
Deploy the inference endpoint in the region geographically closest to each vehicle to minimise round-trip latency
Use Cloud CDN to cache model predictions near the vehicle
Increase the telemetry sampling rate so the cloud detects events sooner

cases.explanation: A hard sub-second requirement combined with intermittent connectivity means the cloud cannot be in the critical path at all - if the link is down, a cloud-dependent alert simply never arrives. Inference moves to the edge, and the cloud takes the roles that tolerate latency: training, model distribution, and analytics.

why_wrong.B: Regional proximity reduces latency but does nothing when there is no connectivity, which the case states is routine.
why_wrong.C: Predictions are computed per vehicle from live sensor state; they are not cacheable content.
why_wrong.D: A higher sampling rate increases bandwidth and cost without addressing either the latency budget or the disconnection problem.

cases.stem: KnightMotives has modest rack compute at 140 depots and needs a managed, remotely updatable runtime there to host containerised inference workloads, consistent with its cloud environment. Which option fits best?

options.t: Google Distributed Cloud at the depots, managed as part of a GKE fleet with Config Sync delivering workload and policy configuration
Install a different Linux distribution at each depot and manage it with SSH scripts
Run all inference in the nearest Google Cloud region and accept the network dependency
Deploy Cloud Run at each depot

cases.explanation: Google Distributed Cloud extends Google Cloud infrastructure to edge and on-premises locations with a managed Kubernetes runtime that can be registered into a fleet, so the same GitOps configuration and policy pipeline manages depot workloads and cloud workloads together, with centrally driven updates.

why_wrong.B: Bespoke per-site management across 140 depots is the operational toil the requirement rules out.
why_wrong.C: This reintroduces the network dependency the sub-second and offline requirements explicitly exclude.
why_wrong.D: Cloud Run is a fully managed Google Cloud service; it cannot be deployed onto customer hardware at a depot.

cases.stem: KnightMotives wants to cut the time from model retraining to fleet-wide rollout from months to days, with the ability to roll back a bad model quickly. Which approach should you recommend?

options.t: An automated Vertex AI Pipelines workflow that trains, evaluates against a held-out set, registers the model version in Model Registry only if it beats the incumbent, then rolls it out in stages to vehicle cohorts with the previous version retained for rollback
Have data scientists email the serialised model to platform engineers when training completes
Push every newly trained model to the entire fleet immediately so improvements reach drivers fastest
Retrain models directly on each vehicle using its own data

cases.explanation: This is the MLOps answer: an automated pipeline with an evaluation gate ensures only models that demonstrably improve on the incumbent are registered, Model Registry provides versioning, and staged rollout to cohorts limits blast radius while keeping the prior version available for immediate rollback.

why_wrong.B: Manual handoff is the current process producing quarter-long lead times.
why_wrong.C: Fleet-wide immediate rollout with no evaluation gate or staging means a regression reaches 900,000 safety-critical systems at once.
why_wrong.D: On-vehicle training on local data gives no fleet-wide learning, no consistency, and no governance, on hardware unsuited to training.

cases.stem: KnightMotives operates in markets with differing data residency rules, and telemetry includes driver identity and location. Which two controls should the design include? (Choose 2.)

options.t: Apply the resource location organisation policy constraint per market folder, and deploy regional resources so telemetry for a market is stored and processed only in permitted regions
Use Sensitive Data Protection to de-identify driver identifiers before telemetry lands in the cross-market analytics dataset
Store all telemetry in a single multi-region bucket and filter by market at query time
Grant analysts in each market the roles/viewer role at the organisation level

cases.explanation: Residency is enforced structurally: the resource location constraint prevents resources being created outside permitted regions, and regional rather than multi-region resources keep data in place. De-identifying driver identifiers before aggregation means the cross-market analytics dataset does not carry personal data across jurisdictions in the first place.

why_wrong.C: A multi-region bucket physically replicates data across regions, so query-time filtering does not satisfy a residency requirement - the data has already moved.
why_wrong.D: Organisation-level viewer grants each market's analysts visibility into every other market's data, which breaches both least privilege and residency intent.

cases.stem: KnightMotives analysts currently extract CSVs from 900 TB of historical telemetry in Cloud Storage and work locally. They need interactive SQL analytics over the full history, plus low-latency lookups of recent per-vehicle state. Which combination should you propose?

options.t: Bigtable for recent per-vehicle state with a TTL-based garbage collection policy, and BigQuery for historical analytics, with telemetry written to both from the streaming pipeline
BigQuery alone, serving both the analytics and the per-vehicle lookups
Bigtable alone, serving both recent lookups and historical SQL analytics
Keep the CSV extract workflow but move the files to a faster storage class

cases.explanation: These are two genuinely different access patterns. Bigtable serves single-key reads of recent state in single-digit milliseconds, with TTL garbage collection keeping the hot dataset small, while BigQuery provides interactive SQL over the full history with partitioning to control cost. Writing to both from one streaming pipeline is the standard fan-out.

why_wrong.B: BigQuery point lookups take seconds and are billed per query, which is unacceptable for per-vehicle state reads at fleet scale.
why_wrong.C: Bigtable has no SQL joins or ad hoc analytical query capability; analysts could not do interactive analysis on it.
why_wrong.D: Local CSV extracts remain unscalable, ungoverned, and stale regardless of the storage class.

cases.stem: Telemetry storage and query costs are growing with the fleet. Historical telemetry is queried heavily for the last 90 days and rarely afterwards, though it must remain queryable. What should you do?

options.t: Partition the BigQuery table by ingestion date, cluster on vehicle identifier, and set a partition expiration or rely on long-term storage pricing for partitions untouched for 90 days
Delete telemetry older than 90 days
Move all telemetry to Archive storage in Cloud Storage and stop using BigQuery
Purchase a larger BigQuery slot reservation to make old queries cheaper

cases.explanation: Partitioning restricts scans to the date ranges a query actually needs, which is the dominant cost lever under on-demand pricing, and clustering on vehicle identifier prunes further. BigQuery automatically applies long-term storage pricing - roughly half - to partitions not modified for 90 days, so the cold data gets cheaper without leaving BigQuery.

why_wrong.B: The requirement states the data must remain queryable, so deletion is out.
why_wrong.C: Moving everything to Archive and abandoning BigQuery destroys the interactive analytics capability the analysts need.
why_wrong.D: A larger reservation increases committed cost; it does not reduce the volume of data scanned.

cases.stem: Before rolling a new safety model to the fleet, KnightMotives wants evidence that the edge inference stack degrades safely when a depot loses its uplink to Google Cloud for an extended period. What should they do?

options.t: Run a controlled chaos experiment in a non-production depot that severs the uplink for a defined period, with a stated hypothesis about continued local inference and buffering, a bounded blast radius, and an abort condition
Review the architecture diagram with the platform team and document the expected behaviour
Run a load test against the cloud ingestion endpoint at three times peak volume
Enable more verbose logging at the depots and wait for a real outage

cases.explanation: The claim being tested is that the system degrades gracefully when disconnected, and the only way to get evidence rather than belief is to induce the failure under controlled conditions. A stated hypothesis, bounded blast radius, and abort condition are what make the experiment safe to run.

why_wrong.B: A design review captures intended behaviour, which is exactly the assumption that needs testing.
why_wrong.C: Load testing the cloud endpoint tests a different failure mode entirely and says nothing about disconnected operation.
why_wrong.D: Waiting for a real outage means discovering the flaw during a genuine incident, with safety-critical consequences.
